nodes.answer: The specific aim is to draw attention to species at risk of localized extinctions in modern urban landscapes.
nodes.paragraph: Abstract Inadequacies in public protected area networks dictates that private land will play an important role in the conservation of biodiversity in the coming decades. Household gar - dens are a key example of private lands that can serve as refuges for biodiversity, with birds as a popular flagship for garden biodiversity. Discussion has focused heavily on the species of plant a resident might select to attract birds to their garden. In this paper, we describe additional and important factors that should form part of this broader conversation on gardens for birds and biodiversity, with a specific aim of drawing attention to species that are at risk of localised extinctions in modern urban landscapes urban adaptors. We present our commentary in two themes: (a) mitigating threats to birds in the urban environ- ment and (b) enhancing the habitat value of the urban environment for a broader range of bird species. We provide a synthesis of the research of recent years that has explored the urban environment and its ability to support birds, but importantly, we extend on this by bringing together topics that have been somewhat lacking in the discussion to date.

nodes.question: What role do remnant green spaces play in urban environments for sensitive species?
nodes.answer: Remnant green spaces facilitate gene flow for species sensitive to urban pressures, acting as corridors and providing essential structural elements like grazing vegetation and large trees.
nodes.paragraph: These barriers reshape the physical landscape and influence species con- nections to their environment, ultimately restructur - ing the functional ecology of habitats (Auffret et al. 2015). The impact of these barriers varies depend- ing on the behavioural and ecological sensitivity of a species, which create a complex interaction between landscape composition and subsequent gene flow (Garrido-Gardu o et al. 2016). Remnant green spaces play a critical role in facilitating gene flow for spe- cies sensitive to urban pressures, acting as corridors or providing essential structural elements like graz- ing vegetation and large trees (Auffret et al. 2015; Christie and Knowles 2015; Regolin et al. 2021). Large-bodied terrestrial mammals with extensive home ranges are particularly reliant on these spaces and are more vulnerable to negative genetic outcomes (e.g., genetic differentiation) due to habitat fragmen- tation (Berger-Tal and Saltz 2019; Lino et al. 2019). As a result, this fragmentation can lead to reduced genetic diversity, inbreeding, and decreased adapt- ability to environmental changes (Frankham 2005; Goldingay et al. 2013), which may cause extirpa- tion in these urbanising landscapes (Ceballos et al 2017).
